course: This course includes 13 analysis papers that you need to write every Sunday at 10pm. At times, it felt like such a burden; I had no time to rest during the weekends. But in the end, I improved at reading philosophical texts, understanding them, and thinking critically about the arguments, then writing about them. We are learning how to think critically, which is a challenging skill to acquire. It is understandable that the course is demanding because, unless it is demanding, you cannot develop this skill properly. This course also helped me improve my time management skills; it taught me I can write good short papers in 1-2 days, which is something I didn't know I could do. It made me realize my potential was more than I thought. Overall, I am very satisfied with this course and my growth. Comparing my initial analysis paper with the latter ones, the improvement is remarkable.

It is really important to engage in this sort of course material as a grad student to learn and understand the fundamental discussions. This course isn't even in my field but I had so much fun doing all the work that it didn't once feel like a burden. I enjoyed coming to class and don't think I have missed any. Even though Simon is an excellent person, I think that most of the topics covered in the course are pointless discussions. Therefore, it would be more appropriate if the articles covered each week were chosen to be more interesting and worthy of discussion. It should also be taken into account that reviewing articles every week in a compulsory PhD course is a huge burden considering the weight of other courses and the intensity of other tasks for someone who works outside.
course: I have no negative thoughts. (Olumsuz düşüncem yok.)

It was an interesting and refreshing course for me, especially the philosophy side of the debates. I liked that we use different system for the assignments that allowed us to see what our friends write which really fostered discussion during the class.

Hukuk öğrencilerinin sosyal bilimlerde araştırma tekniklerini içeren bir dersi almalarının tez çalışmalarına herhangi bir katkısı olduğunu düşünmüyorum. The course workload is too heavy. I don't think it is right that we have an assignment obligation every week for graduate courses. The fact that these assignments are graded causes students to get disenchanted with the course. The course curriculum is also unsuitable for a law PhD program. Considering that our country's rules of law are based on positivist norms, I have difficulty reconciling the values we acquired in the course with our current legal practice. I am not sure if I have learned principles from this course that I can integrate into my professional career. While I support law students learning philosophy, this should be done through classical fields such as philosophy of law or political philosophy. As a PhD student in law who also works full-time in a law office, I found it very difficult to keep up with the assignments and follow the topics, and unfortunately, I lost interest in the course in the process.

The course is so interesting only aspect is since there are a lot of people from pols/philosophy departments the other departments such as management may have had a harder time in keeping up with them. However, even that is very very slight and the professor helped everyone feel so included. Just the technical parts that are unfamiliar with other departments may be the only weak aspect.

strongest= it taught a lot
weakest=some topics were not interesting for me

The most positive aspect of the course was meeting a professor like Simon because he is usually very positive and attentive to his students. But the most negative aspect was that the articles analyzed were for philosophy students more and not easily interesting for other disciplines.

The course was indeed gave me a good notion of philosophy of social sciences. It taught me how to demonstrate professional skepticism and employ different ideas to conduct my research. I very much enjoyed this course, thank you!

Simon hoca treats every student's view with respect and did great in making philosophy as accessible as possible. He makes sure to read everyone's comments for the weekly assignments and encourages active participation by pointing to specific ideas that a student feels comfortable to discuss.

Simon is able to make a complicated and boring subject very interesting. I like that he does not see himself or the subject as bigger than it should be and can make a joke out of things. His examples and explanations are also fun and easy to understand. He has no weak points.
Simon's amazing- he's well informed, invokes interest in the topic always, immensely funny, and respectful and is overall an incredible mind. It was so great to take this class from him.

Simon was a fantastic instructor. Although the composition of the class was quite diverse (students from PHIL, POLS, MAN and LAW) he involved almost all of the students in the discussion. I was quite impressed with how much Simon came prepared to the class having read the papers / comments 10+ students submitted overnight. He was very receptive to questions on course material and obviously is immensely knowledgeable about the subject. 

Certainly not a "weak point" but in terms of feedback it would have been good if we got some earlier visibility on our grades for weekly assignments. Simon assured us that they were fine and there was nothing systemically wrong about them but I think a grade can also be a good indicator (though in his defence, the second week of the class was on the seduction of quantification and how it can go wrong).
course: There is no strong aspect to this course. The weak aspects are way too many. Taking the same philosophy class with people who studied philosophy during bachelors and being expected the same result is way too ridicilious and puts a lot of pressure on us. Weekly readings and papers are way too difficult. There were many weeks I couldn't focus on my own classes from my faculty because of the workload of this class. If this class was not obligatory, I would never choose it.

I think the course does grant a good perspective for looking at / questioning things in social science studies in ways that may not be immediately apparent / intuitive to students from other disciplines. That said the course is quite complicated and I don't know if it can run this smoothly w/o Simon at the helm. Using Perusall was entertaining and did promote early discussion between us before we came to the class. 

In terms of feedback for the course, I've looked at previous reviews and much has been said on the number of assignments and course load. I think a key way to address this (if reducing the work load is not an option) would be to make available to the students an "example analysis paper" and an "example term paper" at the very beginning so that students can align themselves accordingly. 

A final point (that also feeds the point above re the course load) could be explaining how a PHIL weekly assignment would look like at the very beginning. In some disciplines (e.g. law), in-class discussion at an undergraduate level typically revolves around one right answer and the way / ways one can get to said right answer. In a PHIL class however there is no right answer and it's all about how you get to your own, unique conclusion and how it stands when tested against others' views.

The strongest part of the course is that the requirements, workload, and structure was clearly communicated from the start. As a non-philosophy major, I was worried that I would not be able to follow everything. But Simon hoca made sure to have everyone join the conservation and find a topic of interest for the essay, that would still be in line with the philosophical content of the class.
The course created an environment of discussion and pushed the class into thinking and evaluating aspects they have not thought about before

Dersin düzenli ödev yapısı faydalı olmakla birlikte zaman planlaması bakımından bazen zorlayıcıydı ama keyifliydi. Yazdıklarımızın hoca tarafından özenle takip edilmesi ve derste katılım sağlarken de fikirlerimizi beyan edebilmemiz çok kıymetli.

It's a great course but people who are not social scientists taking this course often do not understand the background or methodologically talked about in the class so it may be a little challenging and/or boring for them.

The strongest part of the course is that it can make you question basically everything and anything. It strengthens your analytical thinking. I had no knowledge about philosophy; therefore, sometimes it was hard for me to make references to philosophers and come up with philosophical explanations, which was my own weakness, not that of the class.

You learn a lot in this course and experience a lot of development from the beginning to the end. However, the coursework is time-consuming. The texts are heavy so it takes a lot of time to understand.

The course content is very intensive and involves a lot of reading. Having assignments every week becomes exhausting after a while. For undergraduates, when dealing with many other courses, there's not much that makes a course with so much reading and assignments appealing unless you have an incredible interest in it. Additionally, the grade distribution for all this assignment is low, and the participation requirement is very high, making it less worthwhile to put in so much effort.

There are weekly assignments, so you really have to study weekly and learn even if you do not want to. If you are uninterested with the topic, it will be harder obviously. There will be grad students who will talk about current and older political issues carelessly, so you also learn to be patient towards them. It is a nice life lesson. You also will be immuned to poorest comments from them, and be hopeful about your graduate application. This is the general issue with all philosophy classes, and I think professors should not allow grad students to dominate the class IF their contribution is poor. Also, there were weekly handouts which were really helpful.

instructor: Simon Wigley is a great instructor. He is clearly passionate about philosophy and his expertise exceeds the level of this course. However, I experienced some difficulty in adapting to his teaching style. As a law student, I struggled to participate in class discussions. These discussions might be more accessible if they were moderated in a more guided manner by the instructor.

Simon's wonderfully articulated, communicative and respectful. There's no reason to shy away from taking classes from him just because he is strict about the rules or whatever, he's actually very, very sweet.
